opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underappreciated factors. When people talk about AI in healthcare, they usually focus on the technical side: can the model read the scan, can it predict deterioration, is it accurate enough. But medicine has a very deep professional culture, and that culture shapes whether a tool actually gets used, even when it works.

Part of it is how doctors are trained. It's a long apprenticeship where you're taught that you are personally responsible for the patient. Your judgment is the thing that matters, and if something goes wrong, it's your name on the chart and your license on the line. So when an AI system says "this patient is at high risk," the natural question is: why should I trust that? Who's accountable if it's wrong? If the model can't explain itself in terms that fit how a clinician reasons, it feels like being asked to hand over responsibility without control.

There's also a strong culture of evidence. Physicians are trained to trust randomized trials, peer-reviewed results, and guidelines from their specialty societies. A tech company saying "our model has a high AUC on a retrospective dataset" doesn't carry the same weight. And honestly, that skepticism is often healthy, because a lot of models that look great on historical data don't hold up when you deploy them in a different hospital with different patients and workflows.

Then there's workflow and time. Doctors are already overwhelmed by alerts, documentation, and the EHR. Many have been burned by "smart" tools that turned out to be another pop-up to click through. So there's a learned cynicism: is this going to save me time, or is it one more thing? If an AI tool adds friction, it'll be ignored no matter how good it is.

Identity matters too. Diagnosis, the pattern recognition and clinical intuition, is close to the core of what it means to be a good doctor. Some resistance is less "I don't trust the machine" and more "what is my role if the machine does this part?" That's very human.

So I don't think the answer is to treat that culture as an obstacle to bulldoze. The approaches that work bring clinicians in early, design around their real workflow, validate prospectively in their own setting, and position AI as something that takes away drudgery, like documentation, triage, or surfacing things that are easy to miss, rather than something that replaces their judgment. When doctors feel it makes them better at their job and gives them more time with patients, adoption follows. When it feels imposed from outside, the culture pushes back, and often for good reasons.

r001.rationale: The response says doctors are trained to rely on their own judgment and clinical intuition, and explains that an AI recommendation can feel like surrendering responsibility without control.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to understand is that medicine's professional culture isn't a bug in the system that happens to slow AI down. It's a feature that evolved for very good reasons, and that's exactly what makes it so hard to work around.

Doctors are trained from day one in a culture of individual accountability. When something goes wrong with a patient, there is a name on the chart, and that name is responsible. Years of training reinforce the idea that your judgment is the thing that matters, and that you don't outsource it. So when a tool comes along and says, "Here's what I think the diagnosis is," the instinctive reaction isn't curiosity. It's something closer to, "And who's holding the bag if you're wrong? Because it's going to be me."

That liability asymmetry is huge. If a doctor follows an AI recommendation and it turns out to be wrong, they get blamed. If they ignore the AI and are right, nothing happens. If they ignore the AI and are wrong, well, that's the status quo, and the system already knows how to handle that. So the rational move for an individual clinician, given the incentives, is often to not lean on the tool at all. The culture and the legal structure reinforce each other.

The second piece is epistemology. Medicine has a very specific idea of what counts as evidence. Randomized controlled trials, peer review, mechanisms you can explain. A model that gets a better AUC on a retrospective dataset doesn't fit that framework. Clinicians will ask, "Why did it say that?" and if the honest answer is "we don't fully know," that lands very differently in a hospital than it does in a tech company. In Silicon Valley, "it works empirically" is a win. In medicine, that sentence makes people nervous, and I think they're not entirely wrong to be nervous.

Then there's the hierarchy and the apprenticeship model. Medical knowledge is passed down through attendings and residents, through case conferences, through this very human, very relational process. AI tools often arrive from the outside, from the IT department or from a vendor, with no champion inside that hierarchy. If a respected senior physician in a department doesn't believe in it, it doesn't matter how good the model is. Adoption in medicine spreads through trust networks, not through product features.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that doctors have been burned before. Electronic health records were sold as a tool to help clinicians, and for a lot of them it turned into hours of clicking boxes every night at home. So there's a well-earned skepticism when someone shows up saying this new technology will save you time. The culture has a memory.

Where I've seen things actually work is when AI is framed not as replacing judgment but as extending it in ways that feel consistent with how doctors already think. Ambient documentation is a good example, because it attacks the thing they hate most and doesn't touch their diagnostic authority. Or tools that surface something a clinician would want to see anyway, like a missed follow-up, in a way that feels like a good nurse or a sharp resident flagging something, not a black box issuing verdicts.

So my short answer is that the culture isn't the obstacle you have to defeat. It's the terrain you have to design for. The teams that treat clinician skepticism as irrational resistance tend to fail. The teams that take it seriously as a set of legitimate professional norms, and build for accountability, explainability, and trust from the inside, are the ones that actually get used.

r001.rationale: The response says doctors’ training reinforces that their own judgment matters and should not be outsourced, identifying this self-reliance as a reason they resist AI recommendations.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that medicine is a profession built around expertise and responsibility. Doctors spend years developing their judgment, and they’re accountable for what happens to the patient. So when you introduce an AI system, you’re asking them to trust something whose reasoning they may not be able to inspect, while they still carry the responsibility if it’s wrong. That’s a difficult proposition.

There’s also a tension around professional autonomy. If a tool feels like it’s telling a doctor how to practice, or allowing an administrator to second-guess their decisions, you can understand why they would resist it. That’s different from a tool that helps them find relevant information or spend less time on paperwork.

So I wouldn’t frame this simply as doctors being resistant to technology. The question is whether the technology earns their trust and fits the way they care for patients. You need to involve clinicians in its development, demonstrate where it helps, and make its limitations clear. Adoption becomes much easier when doctors see it as supporting their judgment and their relationship with the patient.

r001.rationale: The response says doctors build their judgment over years and explains that trusting an AI recommendation with opaque reasoning is difficult while they remain accountable. This connects their experience-based clinical judgment to resistance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that medicine is a profession built around expertise, judgment, and personal responsibility. Doctors spend years learning to make decisions, and they’re accountable for what happens to the patient. So when you introduce an AI system, you’re asking them to trust something whose reasoning they may not be able to inspect, while they still carry the responsibility if it’s wrong.

There’s also a tension around autonomy. If a tool feels like it’s second-guessing the physician or telling them how to practice, you can get resistance—even if it performs well on a benchmark. That doesn’t necessarily mean doctors are opposed to technology. They need to see that it works for their patients, fits their workflow, and helps them exercise their judgment.

So I think adoption depends a lot on how you introduce it. Helping with documentation or bringing relevant information to a doctor’s attention can be an easier starting point. You build trust through useful, reliable assistance, and involve clinicians in deciding where the system should—and shouldn’t—have a role.

r001.rationale: The response discusses doctors’ expertise, judgment, accountability, and possible resistance to tools that second-guess them, but does not clearly identify confidence in their own experience-based clinical judgment as the reason they resist AI recommendations.
